content.title: Is Steph Curry Retiring? Warriors Star Shuts Down Rumors After Friday's Loss
content.text: Sources: Barring renewed faith, Steve Kerr not expected to return to Warriors originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay AreaSAN FRANCISCO – One more season. One last chance to prove the Warriors still had the goods to win a couple of playoff series and perhaps even reach the NBA Finals.AdvertisementThat’s all Steve Kerr wanted and believed he could have, according to multiple league sources.Kerr arrived at training camp mentally prepared for the 2025-26 NBA season to close his 12-year tenure as head coach of the Warriors. Whispers heard around the NBA last summer were reinforced when Kerr quickly and firmly dismissed the idea of extending his contract.“I’m very comfortable just going into this season with a year left,” Kerr said last September. “I’m so aligned with (general manager Mike Dunleavy) and (CEO Joe Lacob). There’s no reason for discussion or concern. This is kind of a point in our relationship where it’s like, let’s just see how it is at the end of the year.”The end of the year came last Friday, when Golden State’s season of torment was euthanized in a play-in tournament loss to the Phoenix Suns.AdvertisementThe general belief among the Warriors – openly expressed by Draymond Green – and around the league since the weekend is that Kerr will be comfortably jobless after meeting with Lacob and Dunleavy. Most expect a decision in a matter of days, not weeks.Yet Kerr last week left open the possibility – very slight, according to sources – of returning. Multiple sources indicate his decision, however, will not be based on the dollar amount.“They could offer Steve $25 million a year,” one league source said, “and I doubt that alone would make a difference.”Two sources insist that any change of heart would require, among other factors, Kerr having renewed faith in his role as the franchise shifts toward the future.AdvertisementTen years ago, when the Warriors posted their record 73-9 regular season, Kerr introduced the most effective “small ball” unit in NBA history. With 6-foot-6 Green at center, flanked by 6-foot-7 Harrison Barnes and 6-foot-6 Andre Iguodala on the wings, with 6-foot-6 Klay Thompson joining 6-foot-3 Stephen Curry, Golden State had the birth of the “Death Lineup.”That highly switchable lineup used speed and smarts to demolish opponents with defense and demoralize them with transition offense often punctuated by 3-pointers.Kerr was celebrated for recognizing the defense/offense potency of that squad and then utilizing it to astonishing success.One year later, the Warriors super-sized that squad, replacing Barnes with 6-foot-11 Kevin Durant, and ransacked opponents to such a degree they earned a nickname: “Super Villains.”AdvertisementKerr’s system and the skills of the players revolutionized the NBA. Other teams tried to mimic them only to realize they couldn’t match the fireworks of the Curry-Thompson backcourt and had no one with Draymond’s combination of speed, intellect and defensive versatility.Much has changed since Golden State ruled the league. Durant and Thompson joined other teams. Iguodala retired. Curry and Green remain Warriors, but they’re closer to 40 than 30. These Warriors have difficulty transcending mediocrity.Meanwhile, the rest of the league is getting bigger, stronger, quicker and younger. Kerr, this season, coached a team that struggled to keep up even before it was hit with a dizzying spate of injuries. And even he concedes this was not his best work.Kerr came out of training camp seeing a chance for the Warriors to compete at the highest level. His early optimism was based mostly on his faith in four people: Jimmy Butler III, Curry, Green and Dr. Rick Celebrini, Golden State’s vice president of health and performance.AdvertisementThis would be the year to touch greatness or at least some close. This roster was assembled for a single-season run, and that was Kerr’s mentality.The Warriors hoarded veterans with one-year obligations. De’Anthony Melton and 39-year-old Al Horford both signed deals with player options for next season. Seth Curry and Gary Payton II, who now are bound for unrestricted free agency.This roll of the dice was made with the hope that Curry’s timeless brilliance and the roster’s collective experience could overcome acute deficiencies in athleticism and size.Celebrini, by all accounts, is marvelous at his job. And, still, Golden State’s season was wrecked by injuries and conditions beyond his control.AdvertisementThe worst fears of Lacob, Dunleavy and Kerr were that the decorated vets atop the roster would incur substantial absences. And that’s what happened with three of them. Butler missed 44 games, 38 after sustaining a torn right ACL in mid-January. Curry missed 39 games, 27 after being diagnosed with runner’s knee in late January. Horford missed 37 games with an assortment of injuries. Green was the most available, missing 14 games.Golden State’s season went from mediocre in the first two months, to warming in the third month, to hearing a death knell over the final three. Kerr always was scrambling for workable solutions; he used 43 different starting lineups and seemingly 400 different rotations.Nothing Kerr did made the Warriors any better. What it did was expose an abjectly deficient roster surrounding Curry and Butler.Several times during the season, after a seemingly avoidable defeat, Kerr would take the blame, saying he needed to be better. He was right. Injuries gave him a horrible hand, but he seemed exasperated with his inability to stem the consistency of his team’s self-mutilating turnovers. It was as if he were resigned to living with them, though he did discuss with Draymond the nasty habit that followed him early in the season.AdvertisementThis was not the coach who brought consistent engagement to the franchise in 2014, when he was installing an offense based on movement of ball and bodies and showed no restraint in barking at the star point guard – Curry – to be more mindful.Maybe Kerr last season reached the point of exasperation. Or exhaustion. He seemed to accept what we all could see. The hits kept coming, the team kept sliding and disappointment registered from the fan base to the offices at Chase Center. There was a sense of despair.Kerr longed for a season that ended in smiles. It’s quite the romantic notion. Kerr’s desire for one more year came and went without glory. And the widespread belief is he is uninterested in an encore to what he hoped would be an encore.Download and follow the Dubs Talk Podcast
